posts.text:
Countries usually grow by conquering their neighbors.

The Netherlands grew by conquering the sea.

This map shows what the country looked like in 1300 vs today — a thread 🧵🗺️

1/ Every pale area on the map was water or marsh in 1300.

About a sixth of the modern Netherlands has been pulled out of the sea, lake by lake — and roughly a quarter of the country now sits BELOW sea level, kept dry by pumps that can never stop.

2/ The tools: dikes, then windmills. From the 1400s the Dutch used wind power to pump polders dry.

The Beemster polder (1612) — a lake turned into farmland with 43 windmills — was such a feat of engineering it's now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

3/ The masterpiece is the map's center: the Zuiderzee, an inland sea, was sealed off by the 32 km Afsluitdijk in 1932.

Out of its bed rose Flevoland — home to 400,000+ people and, since 1986, the country's newest province. Most of it didn't exist a century ago.

4/ The sea fought back. In 1953 a North Sea storm surge broke the southern dikes, drowned 1,836 people and forced 100,000 from their homes.

The response — the Delta Works — is a 40-year system of dams and movable barriers often called one of the wonders of the modern world.

5/ The result is a country that maintains itself like a machine: Schiphol Airport lies ~4 m below sea level, and the old saying is earned, not boastful:

"God created the world, but the Dutch created the Netherlands."

6/ As seas rise, the world is coming to Dutch engineers for advice — 800 years of practice, mapped above.

Follow @forummapping for more maps like this.
